title: Coquilles Saint-Jacques
subtitle: Scallops in a cream and white wine sauce, finished with gratin
excerpt: Scallops gently cooked in white wine with mushrooms and shallots, folded into a cream sauce, returned to their shells, topped with breadcrumbs, and finished under the grill. A classic French dinner-party dish.
sourceNotes: Coquilles Saint-Jacques au gratin is a classic of the French classical and bourgeois repertoire. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), gives the full classical preparation. The dish is named for the scallop shell carried by pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago (Saint James's Way), the French name for Saint James is Saint Jacques. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives the home-cook version.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The scallop filling can be made up to 2 hours ahead and held in the shells in the fridge. Bring to room temperature before grilling.

glossaryTerms.definition: A French technique of finishing a dish under a hot grill to create a browned, crisp top layer. Gratins can be topped with breadcrumbs, cheese, or a combination of both. The word gratin comes from gratter, 'to scrape' — originally referring to the crisp, scrapeable crust that forms on the surface.

content.text: Coquilles Saint-Jacques is scallops poached briefly in white wine, folded into a cream and mushroom sauce, returned to the shells, sprinkled with breadcrumbs, and finished under the grill as a
. It is one of the most elegant of French dinner-party first courses, and one that can be almost entirely prepared in advance.
Ask your fishmonger to open the scallops and keep the deep half-shells. If you cannot get shells, use small gratin dishes instead.

items.prepNote: shelled and cleaned, roes on if available
finely grated, for the gratin top

content.text: Melt 20 g of the butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the shallots and cook for 3 minutes. Add the finely chopped mushrooms and a large pinch of salt. Cook, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes until all the moisture has evaporated and the mushrooms are dry and starting to colour. Set aside.

In the saucepan, bring the white wine to a simmer. Add the scallops and poach for exactly 2 minutes, they should be just barely cooked and still slightly translucent at the centre. Remove with a slotted spoon. Reserve the poaching liquid.

In the saucepan, melt the remaining 20 g of butter over medium heat. Add the flour and stir for 1 minute. Gradually whisk in the reserved poaching liquid, then the cream. Simmer for 4 minutes until smooth and thick. Season with salt, pepper, and lemon juice.
Stir the mushroom mixture into the sauce.
Divide among the shells or gratin dishes.
Mix the breadcrumbs and parmesan and scatter over each shell. Place under a hot grill for 3 to 4 minutes until the top is golden and the filling is bubbling at the edges.

items.cause: They were poached for too long, scallops toughen very quickly past the 2-minute mark.
items.fix: Next time, err on the side of underdone at the poaching stage; the scallops will finish cooking under the grill. They should be just opaque on the outside and slightly translucent in the centre after poaching.

items.cause: Insufficient reduction, or too much wine was used.
items.fix: Simmer the finished sauce for a further 2 to 3 minutes. It should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon before the scallops go in.

items.symptom: The gratin top is pale after grilling
items.cause: The grill was not hot enough, or the dishes were placed too far from the heat.
items.fix: Preheat the grill for a full 5 minutes at maximum. Place the shells on the top rack as close to the element as possible. Keep watching, the difference between golden and burnt takes less than a minute.

content.text: The scallop shell is the emblem of Saint James and of the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela, which passes through France and northern Spain. The dish has no single regional home in France, appearing along both coasts and on restaurant menus throughout the country. In classical French cuisine it was always one of the set pieces of the gastronomic dinner-party menu, served in the shell as the fish course between the soup and the meat. It remains one of the most recognisably French of dinner-party dishes.
